findings.title: Move large response construction and encoding off the event loop
findings.description: Building up to 75,000 Pydantic records and encoding the resulting response run synchronously after the database executor returns. The load-test notes a ceiling-sized candle response of about 34.8 MB; this work can take far longer than the Python rules’ 1 ms limit for synchronous work inside an async handler and block unrelated requests. The same issue applies to `get_trades`. Offload model construction and serialization to a worker thread, or otherwise ensure this potentially large CPU-bound work does not block the event loop.

findings.title: Count and fetch do not share a consistent snapshot
findings.description: The count and fetch are separate statements on a pooled connection. Under PostgreSQL’s default `READ COMMITTED` isolation, each statement can see a different snapshot, so inserts after the count can make the fetch return more than the configured ceiling. The reader’s claim that this can add only one row is not guaranteed for a concurrent batch insert. Use a consistent snapshot for admission and fetch, or otherwise enforce a hard bound without returning a truncated response. The same count-then-fetch pattern is used by `get_trades`.

findings.title: Document the tape watermark’s actual meaning
findings.description: The `tape_complete_through` field description says it is the created time of the newest stored trade, but `tape_facts()` populates it from the trades sync-state watermark. The schema documents that watermark as the end of the last fully walked window—not the newest stored trade. Since clients may rely on the generated API description to interpret this timestamp, describe it as the completeness watermark.
